# If You Slip {-}

> "Don't rejoice against me, my enemy. When I fall, I will arise."
>
> — Micah 7:8

This short chapter has no number, and I hope you never need it. It is a warning, and it gives no permission. The rule from the final step stands: not once, for any reason.

But the rule is strict and the grace is real. A soldier who trips on the march doesn't desert. He gets up and falls back in. So here is what to do if you fall.

## Am I back to zero? {-}

No. There's no counter in this book, so there's no zero to go back to. Your freedom was never a number. A man in a recovery group pictured it as a row of hurdles. You cleared ten cleanly and stumbled on the eleventh. That doesn't mean you have to go back and start the race again.

But don't shrug it off. Something real happened. You fed the Little Monster and your conscience knows it. It makes no difference whether it was the site, the hand or a message to her. Do three things, in this order.

*Confess it today.* Don't wait until you've punished yourself for a week. "If we confess our sins, he is faithful": you learned that in Chapter 20, and it wasn't only for the first time. Solomon didn't say the righteous man never falls. He said he gets up, seven times if he must. If you're married, tell your wife as well, and tell the man you told. Don't start a new secret. And remember the two words from the final step, spoken to a man who still smelled of yesterday: just come.

*Refuse the second one.* The real danger was never the fall. It's the thought that arrives an hour later: "Well, I've blown it now, so I may as well." That's the streak counter talking. One fall is a fall, and a week of "may as well" puts you back inside. The pang is made of fear. A man who decides he's "hooked for life" after one slip has scared himself back inside.

*Find the lie that crept back.* A fall usually means one of the old lies got back in. You doubted, or you waited, or you kept a substitute, or you "tested" yourself, or you'd kept a way back. The things you learned in this book haven't been unlearned. Find the gap, re-read that chapter, take the final step again and be glad again.

You fell forward.

## The lies that follow a slip {-}

The forums call it a "relapse" and reset the counter. The word does damage of its own. It turns one stupid act into an identity: *I'm a relapser.* What actually happened is smaller. You slipped, you fed the Little Monster, and now the Big Monster is telling you lies. Learn to recognize them.

- **"I'll never be free."** One slip has become a life sentence. Would you say that to a friend?
- **"From now on I must be perfect: up at five, cold shower, an hour of prayer, no sugar."** Here guilt has dressed itself up as discipline. You'll keep it up for four days, collapse, and reach for comfort.
- **"Other men are on day two hundred and I can't manage twenty. I must be a hopeless case."** You're comparing yourself with a number on a stranger's screen. You don't know how he's doing, and it doesn't matter.
- **"I shouldn't even feel desire."** Yes, you should. Desire is God's idea, as Chapter 3 said. You're a man and not a statue. Noticing that a woman is beautiful is not a fall. The sin was never the noticing. It was the taking.

Every one of those thoughts feels like repentance, and none of them is. Repentance is quick and it faces forward.

## Wanting it to hurt {-}

Religious men get one snare all to themselves.

A man follows this method and finds stopping easy. Then he feels guilty that it was easy. Surely, after all those years, it ought to cost something. Surely he should suffer a little, by way of payment. So some part of him sets about making it hard. He broods and punishes himself. He even half welcomes a fall, so that he can feel properly wretched afterward.

See that for what it is. It's the old lie in a hair shirt. If you're a Christian you know perfectly well who paid, and it wasn't you. Trying to add your own suffering to the bill isn't humility. The debt was cleared in full. You don't owe misery on top, so take the freedom and be glad of it.

## The men who quit the pebble {-}

If a slip has left you taking the whole business very solemnly, here's some medicine. EasyPeasy borrows a parody from a writer called Guillaco, who imagined a support forum for people trying to give up drinking bleach. The idea is borrowed here, with thanks, and the poison changed. Meet the brave men of a made-up forum, who are trying to stop walking around with a sharp pebble in their shoe.

"Day 19 pebble-free. Walked past a gravel drive this morning and nearly lost it. Stay strong, brothers."

"I allow myself the pebble on Sundays only. I think that's a healthy balance."

"Honestly, how is a man supposed to stop? I've always got feet. I've always got shoes. The temptation is with me every waking hour."

"I was doing so well. Then I had a stressful week at work and before I knew it I was in the yard, picking one out. A small one. I'm so ashamed. Resetting my counter."

"Does anyone else find the limp sort of comforting?"

"My accountability partner checks my shoes every Friday. So far so good, though I did think about the beach all through the sermon."

You're smiling because you can see what they can't. Nobody needs courage, a counter or a Friday inspection to keep a pebble out of his shoe. All he needs is to notice that it hurts and that it never did a thing for him. Once he's seen that, leaving it out isn't an achievement. It's just walking.

How many times this week were you tempted to put a stone in your shoe? None. That isn't self-control. You see a stone for what it is.

If you slipped, the lesson is not "try harder". Somewhere you started believing again that the pebble had something to offer. Find where, go back to that chapter, and read it again. Reading this book a second time is no disgrace and takes only a few hours. The world repeats its lies daily, so it does no harm to hear the truth twice.
